title: Making Noisy F1 Data Move Like a Car
summary: Sepang Vision Lab replays the 2026 Sepang weekend in 3D from public OpenF1 data. Most of the work went into making sparse, jittery positions move like a real car without inventing anything.
postscript: You are the one who inspired me to do this. I hope you see Russell win, so I can see you smile.

related.label: Sepang Vision Lab: the case study
Where AI Belongs in a Data Quality Workflow

body: I like how Formula 1 uses data to understand performance. When OpenF1 published the 2026 Sepang weekend, I wanted to see how much of it I could rebuild from public data alone: every practice session, qualifying and the race, with all 22 cars driving an aligned 3D model of the circuit.
The 3D part turned out to be the easier half.

value.caption: The race replay on the TV camera: the timing tower for all 22 cars, a safety car message, the track map and weather.

body: OpenF1 publishes car positions at about four samples a second, with jittery timestamps, in a coordinate system that matches no map. Played back as they arrive, the cars stutter, cut corners, overlap and float above the track.

value.caption: Twelve real seconds of one car through a corner. Press Play on Raw, then on Smoothed. The histogram is the gap between every sample in that half hour of the race.

value.text: Fix the data before the visuals

body: Most of what looked like rendering bugs came from the data. Fixing it at the source fixed every camera at once.

items: **Alignment.** Positions are fitted to the circuit model with a derived similarity transform, 3.09 m RMS from the centre line.
**Smooth motion.** Each car’s distance along the track and offset across it are refitted against time, so cars follow their real line.
**A physics check.** Sampled at 50 Hz across the race, 99% of frames stay within the braking, acceleration and cornering range of a real car.
**Cars keep their space.** Overlapping cars are eased apart sideways. Overlapping frames in the race fell from 3,955 to 211.

body: Some things the data cannot say. When OpenF1’s tyre labels disagree, the timing tower shows a question mark instead of a guess, and a data gap marks the car as stale after two seconds. Every number is labelled as derived, sourced, official or illustrative. That labelling is what lets a replay be trusted.

value.caption: The chase camera through a corner on lap 9, with the rev arc, gear, g-meter and a stewards message.

body: Earlier versions carried lap-time models and strategy tools. I removed them so the project could do one recorded weekend well. The product became clearer, not smaller.
The one AI feature left has a narrow job. The race engineer answers questions about gaps, tyres, pace and flags only from a brief of recorded data, so it explains the race without inventing it.
The [case study](/projects/sepang-vision-lab) has the architecture and every feature, and the [live replay](https://sepangvisionlab.madebyrazeen.com) is the best way to see it.
